points: We judge behavior as caused by the person (internal) or the situation (external) — Heider, 1958.
Jones & Davis: we infer true traits when behavior is freely chosen and unexpected.
Kelley's model: check consensus, consistency and distinctiveness before judging.
First impressions bias everything that follows — early judgments stick.
Surprising behavior triggers deeper analysis; expected behavior barely gets a thought.
items.title: Attribution Theory

points: We over-blame personality and under-blame situations when judging others (Ross, 1977).
Quizmaster study: random roles made people look smarter than they were.
Actor-observer bias: we excuse our own behavior, but judge others harshly.
Self-serving bias: we take credit for wins and blame circumstances for losses.
Fix it: pause and ask what invisible pressures the other person faces.
items.title: Fundamental Attribution Error

points: Clashes between beliefs and behavior create painful mental tension (Festinger, 1957).
The $1/$20 experiment: tiny rewards changed beliefs; big rewards did not.
Effort justification: the harder we work for something, the more we value it.
After tough choices we boost the winner and trash the loser.
Persuaders use it: small public commitments quietly shift attitudes.
items.title: Cognitive Dissonance

points: Prejudice = stereotypes (beliefs) + emotions (dislike) + readiness to discriminate.
Competition over scarce resources breeds prejudice — Robbers Cave, 1954.
We favor our own group to boost self-esteem (Tajfel's social identity theory).
Allport's contact hypothesis: equal-status teamwork reduces prejudice.
What works: recategorization, perspective-taking and fair institutional rules.
items.title: Prejudice: Roots and Reduction

points: Stereotypes are group shortcuts that distort what we notice and remember.
Stereotype threat: fear of confirming a stereotype hurts performance (Steele & Aronson).
It drains mental resources — affecting many groups in tests and sports.
Reduced by fair framing, role models and a growth mindset.
Media wires automatic associations; diverse portrayals are the antidote.
items.title: Stereotypes and Stereotype Threat

points: The more witnesses to an emergency, the less likely anyone helps (Darley & Latané).
Diffusion of responsibility: “someone else will do it” becomes everyone's excuse.
Pluralistic ignorance: calm faces mislead us into thinking nothing is wrong.
Beat it: point at one specific person and give a direct order.
Knowing about the effect makes you personally less vulnerable to it.
items.title: Bystander Effect

points: Proximity is the #1 predictor — we like people we encounter often.
Mere exposure: repeated contact alone increases liking.
Similarity in values and attitudes predicts lasting relationships.
“What is beautiful is good” — beauty biases first impressions.
We like people who like us — reciprocity is a powerful magnet.
items.title: Attraction: What Draws Us Together

points: Love = intimacy (closeness) + passion (desire) + commitment (decision).
Seven types emerge from different mixes — from liking to consummate love.
Passion peaks early and fades; intimacy grows slowly; commitment stabilizes.
Companionate love predicts long-term satisfaction better than passion.
Diagnose your triangle, then act on whichever piece is missing.
items.title: Sternberg's Triangular Theory of Love

points: Audiences boost performance on easy tasks but hurt hard ones (Triplett, 1898).
Zajonc's drive theory: arousal strengthens our dominant response.
Fear of being judged is the engine — supportive crowds energize.
Golden rule: practice privately, perform publicly.
Even virtual or imagined audiences trigger mild facilitation.
items.title: Social Facilitation

points: People exert less effort in groups than alone (Latané's experiments).
Ringelmann effect: teams underperform the sum of individual efforts.
Causes: hidden effort, dispensability, diffusion of responsibility.
Fix: make every person's contribution visible and evaluated.
Small teams, clear roles and inspiring missions restore effort.
items.title: Social Loafing

points: Anonymity in crowds dissolves self-awareness (Zimbardo).
Uniforms, masks, darkness and crowds all increase it.
The internet is a deindividuation machine — trolling and pile-ons.
Not always destructive: it also fuels charity crowds and concert joy.
Restore restraint with name tags, cameras and accountability.
items.title: Deindividuation

points: Desire for harmony overrides realistic thinking (Janis, 1972).
Eight symptoms: invulnerability illusion, self-censorship, pressure on dissenters.
Bay of Pigs and the Challenger disaster show the tragic pattern.
Cures: devil's advocate, anonymous input, outside experts.
The goal is not less cohesion — it is cohesion plus courage.
items.title: Groupthink in Depth

points: Unwritten rules of behavior, enforced by approval and embarrassment.
Descriptive norms (what people do) beat injunctive norms (what they should do).
Sherif (1936): norms form spontaneously and spread like culture.
Pluralistic ignorance creates false norms everyone privately rejects.
Build good norms: make the desired behavior visible and rewarded.
items.title: Social Norms

points: Roles are the behaviors expected from a position — mother, student, boss.
Stanford Prison Experiment (1971): roles overpowered personality in six days.
Role conflict strikes between roles; role strain strikes within one role.
Emotional labor — faking feelings all day — drains and burns out.
Play roles consciously: you are more than any single role.
items.title: Social Roles

points: Without objective measures, we judge ourselves against others (Festinger, 1954).
Upward comparison inspires — or breeds envy and inadequacy.
Downward comparison protects self-esteem but can breed complacency.
Social media: comparing our reality to everyone's highlight reel.
Healthiest race: compete only against who you were yesterday.
items.title: Social Comparison Theory

points: Central route: logic and evidence — creates lasting change (Petty & Cacioppo).
Peripheral route: attractiveness, music, slogans — fades quickly.
Which route wins depends on motivation × ability to think.
Repetition boosts persuasion — until it backfires.
Defense: demand real evidence before important decisions.
items.title: Persuasion: Central vs Peripheral Routes

points: Foot-in-the-door: a small yes leads to a much bigger yes (1966).
Door-in-the-face: start huge, then retreat to the real request.
Low-balling: agree to a sweet deal, then watch the price rise.
Scarcity and urgency push us from deliberation to impulse.
Resist: recognize the pattern, slow down, judge each request alone.
items.title: Compliance Techniques

points: Conflict = perceived incompatible goals — handled well, it sparks creativity.
Styles: competing, avoiding, accommodating, collaborating.
Principled negotiation: separate people from problems (Fisher & Ury).
BATNA — your best walk-away option — is your real power.
Lasting peace needs fair procedures and shared goals.
items.title: Conflict and Negotiation

points: Individualism prizes independence; collectivism prizes harmony — the biggest split.
Attribution differs: individualists blame persons, collectivists weigh context.
Same behavior, different meaning — “peer pressure” vs “respect for harmony”.
Bicultural people code-switch between mindsets with language.
Cultural intelligence beats assuming everyone thinks like you.
items.title: Culture and Social Behavior

points: Variable rewards — unpredictable likes — work like slot machines.
Curated feeds supercharge harmful upward comparison.
FOMO fragments attention, disrupts sleep and feeds anxiety.
Algorithms build echo chambers: outrage earns engagement.
Healthy use: limit scrolling, curate feeds, keep phones out of bedrooms.
items.title: Social Media Psychology
